title: Memory & State
description: Short-term versus long-term memory, managing a growing context window, scratchpads for working memory, and persisting state across sessions.

lessons.title: Short-Term vs. Long-Term Memory
lessons.description: An agent's working memory for this task and its memory across tasks are different problems with different solutions.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Distinguish short-term (within-task) memory from long-term (across-task) memory and describe how each is typically implemented.

sections.title: ⏱️ Short-term memory: this task's working state
sections.content: The running history of thoughts, actions, and observations within a single agent run — everything covered in the control loop lesson's discussion of 'state.' This lives only for the duration of the current task and is typically just the accumulating context passed into each LLM call, bounded by the context window and possibly summarized once it gets long (the subject of the next lesson).

sections.title: 🗄️ Long-term memory: persisting across tasks
sections.content:
Information that should be available in future, separate interactions — a user's stated preferences, facts learned in a previous session, a summary of past conversations. This can't just live in the current context window, because it needs to survive after the current run ends; it needs to be stored somewhere external (a database, a vector store) and explicitly retrieved when relevant, much like the retrieval step in a RAG pipeline.

```python
# Short-term: lives only in this run's state
state["history"].append((thought, action, observation))

# Long-term: written to durable storage, retrieved by future runs
memory_store.save(user_id, fact="prefers concise answers")
...
# in a LATER, separate session:
relevant = memory_store.retrieve(user_id, query=current_task)
```

sections.title: 🔗 How long-term memory typically works
sections.content: Store discrete facts, summaries, or past interactions with enough metadata to find them again later (timestamps, user IDs, topics). At the start of a new task, retrieve the subset that's relevant to the current situation — often via the same embedding-and-similarity-search approach covered in the Embeddings and RAG courses — rather than trying to load everything ever stored into context, which wouldn't fit and wouldn't all be relevant anyway.

sections.title: ⚖️ Choosing what belongs in which
sections.content: If it only matters for completing the current task and won't be needed again, it belongs in short-term memory (or shouldn't be persisted at all). If it should influence future, separate interactions — a preference, a fact worth remembering, a summary of what happened — it needs to go into long-term storage explicitly; nothing carries over automatically just because a conversation happened.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming anything discussed during a session automatically becomes long-term memory.** Nothing persists past the current run unless it's explicitly written to external storage — an unstated assumption here means a preference the user mentioned simply vanishes.

**Loading everything ever stored into context instead of retrieving a relevant subset.** This wastes context budget on irrelevant history and reintroduces the exact problem retrieval is meant to solve.

**Storing long-term memories with no metadata for finding them again.** A fact saved with no timestamp, user ID, or topic is nearly as good as not saved at all once retrieval needs to narrow down what's actually relevant.

questions.question: What is short-term memory in an agent, as described in this lesson?
options: Information stored permanently in an external database
The running history of thoughts, actions, and observations within a single task's execution
A summary of every past user interaction ever recorded
The model's pretraining data
questions.explanation: Short-term memory is the accumulating context within one task's loop — it exists only for the duration of that run, unlike long-term memory which is meant to persist.

questions.question: Why can't long-term memory simply live in the current context window the way short-term memory does?
options: Long-term memory doesn't actually exist as a concept
It needs to survive after the current run ends, so it must be stored externally and explicitly retrieved later
Context windows are infinite in size
Long-term memory is never useful for agents
questions.explanation: Anything meant to persist across separate future interactions needs external storage (a database or vector store) since the current run's context disappears once the task ends.

questions.question: What approach does this lesson say is commonly used to retrieve relevant long-term memories for a new task?
options: Loading every stored memory into context regardless of relevance
An embedding-and-similarity-search approach similar to RAG's retrieval step
Long-term memories cannot be retrieved once stored
Randomly selecting stored memories
questions.explanation: Rather than loading everything, relevant memories are typically retrieved via similarity search, echoing the same retrieval pattern covered in the Embeddings and RAG courses.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what distinguishes the long-term memory lines from the short-term memory line?
options: The long-term lines write to and read from memory_store, a durable store used across separate sessions, while the short-term line only appends to the current run's state
The short-term line uses a database, while the long-term lines use only in-memory variables
Both examples do exactly the same thing with different variable names
The long-term lines never involve any form of retrieval
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example contrasts state['history'].append (this run only) with memory_store.save/retrieve, which explicitly persist and retrieve information across separate, later sessions.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what is passed to memory_store.retrieve when a later session begins?
options: The user_id and the current task, used as a query
Nothing — retrieve() takes no arguments
Only a timestamp with no other information
The entire history of every user who has ever used the system
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example calls memory_store.retrieve(user_id, query=current_task), retrieving memories relevant to that specific user and situation rather than everything ever stored.

questions.question: Why does this lesson say long-term memory storage should include metadata like timestamps, user IDs, and topics?
options: Because it's needed to find relevant memories again later, rather than trying to load everything ever stored into context
Because metadata makes memories load faster regardless of relevance
Because metadata is required by law for any stored user data
Because without metadata, memories cannot be written to storage at all
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that metadata is what enables retrieving the relevant subset of stored memories later, rather than an unfiltered, unusable dump of everything ever recorded.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against assuming anything discussed during a session automatically becomes long-term memory?
options: Because nothing persists past the current run unless it's explicitly written to external storage, so an unstated preference simply vanishes
Because all conversation content is automatically saved to long-term storage by default in every agent framework
Because short-term memory and long-term memory are actually the exact same mechanism
Because agents are incapable of forgetting anything once a session begins
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is assuming automatic persistence, when anything meant to survive across sessions must be explicitly written to durable, external storage.

questions.question: Why does this lesson caution against loading everything ever stored into context instead of retrieving a relevant subset?
options: Because this wastes context budget on irrelevant history and reintroduces the exact problem retrieval is meant to solve
Because loading everything always produces better results than retrieving a relevant subset
Because context windows have no limit on how much can be loaded at once
Because retrieval is only relevant for short-term memory, never long-term memory
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is skipping retrieval and dumping everything into context, which defeats the purpose of storing memories in a way that supports targeted, relevant retrieval.

lessons.title: Managing the Context Window Over a Long Task
lessons.description: A long-running agent will eventually generate more history than fits in context — you need a plan before that happens, not after.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Describe at least two strategies for managing an agent's growing context over a long-running task.

sections.title: 📈 Why this becomes a problem
sections.content: Building on the context window economics covered in the LLM Engineering course, every thought, action, and observation adds to the state fed into the next LLM call. On a long-running or complex task, this history can grow well past what fits in the model's context window, or past the point where cost and latency (which scale with context length) become a real concern even if it technically still fits.

sections.title: ✂️ Truncation
sections.content:
The simplest approach: drop the oldest history once a length limit is reached, keeping only the most recent steps. Cheap and simple, but risks losing genuinely important early context (an early observation that's still relevant later in the task) purely because it's old, not because it's irrelevant.

```python
def truncate(history, max_items):
    return history[-max_items:]  # keep only the most recent N, oldest dropped
```

sections.title: 📝 Summarization
sections.content:
Periodically compress older history into a shorter summary (using an LLM call to do the summarizing) that preserves the important facts while discarding the verbatim detail — keeping recent steps in full detail and older steps as a summary. This retains more useful information than truncation for a similar token budget, at the cost of an extra LLM call to produce each summary and some risk of the summary itself dropping something that turns out to matter.

```python
def compress(history, keep_recent=10):
    old, recent = history[:-keep_recent], history[-keep_recent:]
    summary = llm.summarize(old)  # extra LLM call, but preserves the gist
    return [summary] + recent
```

sections.title: 🗂️ Selective retention / retrieval-based memory
sections.content: Rather than keeping history in strict chronological order, store the full history externally and use a retrieval step (similar to long-term memory's approach) to pull back only the specific past steps that seem relevant to the current decision, rather than everything or just the most recent items. This handles tasks with long histories where an important early fact needs to remain accessible far later, something truncation and simple summarization both handle less gracefully.

sections.title: 🎯 Choosing an approach
sections.content: Truncation is fine for short, simple tasks where old context is unlikely to matter. Summarization is a good general-purpose default for moderate-length tasks. Retrieval-based selective retention is worth the extra complexity for long, complex tasks where losing an important early detail would be genuinely costly.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Reaching for truncation as the default for every long-running agent.** It's the cheapest option, but this lesson is explicit that it risks losing genuinely important early context purely because of age, not relevance.

**Summarizing on every single step regardless of how much history has actually accumulated.** Each summarization is an extra LLM call — running it more often than the growing history actually requires wastes cost and latency for no added benefit.

**Picking retrieval-based retention for every task 'to be safe.'** Its extra complexity is worth paying specifically for long, complex tasks where an early detail's loss would be costly — for shorter tasks, summarization or even truncation is simpler and sufficient.

questions.question: Why does an agent's context grow over the course of a long-running task?
options: Context size is fixed and never changes
Every thought, action, and observation adds to the state fed into the next LLM call
The model automatically compresses its own history
Agents never accumulate any history
questions.explanation: Each loop iteration's thought, action, and observation gets appended to the running state, which keeps growing as the task continues.

questions.question: What is the main risk of simple truncation (dropping the oldest history) as a context management strategy?
options: It always increases cost compared to keeping everything
It can lose genuinely important early context purely because it's old, not because it's irrelevant
It requires an extra LLM call for every truncation
It's technically impossible to implement
questions.explanation: Truncation is cheap and simple but indiscriminate — it drops old information regardless of whether that information is still needed later in the task.

questions.question: When is retrieval-based selective retention worth its extra complexity compared to summarization?
options: Never — summarization is always sufficient
For long, complex tasks where losing an important early detail would be genuinely costly and truncation/summarization handle that less gracefully
Only for tasks with no tools at all
Only when the context window is unlimited
questions.explanation: Retrieval-based retention specifically helps when a specific early fact needs to stay accessible far later in a long task — a case where truncation and even summarization risk losing it.

questions.question: In this lesson's truncate code example, what does history[-max_items:] return?
options: Only the most recent max_items entries, with the oldest entries dropped
Only the oldest max_items entries, with recent ones dropped
A summary generated by an LLM call
The entire unmodified history with nothing removed
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example uses Python's slice history[-max_items:] to keep only the tail (most recent items) of the history list.

questions.question: In this lesson's compress code example, what is passed to llm.summarize?
options: Only the older portion of history (everything except the most recent keep_recent items)
The entire history including the most recent items
Nothing — llm.summarize takes no arguments
Only a single most recent item
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example splits history into old and recent, then calls llm.summarize(old) — summarizing only the older portion while keeping recent items in full detail.

questions.question: Why does this lesson describe summarization as retaining 'more useful information than truncation for a similar token budget'?
options: Because summarization preserves the important facts from older history rather than discarding it outright the way truncation does
Because summarization always uses fewer tokens than truncation
Because truncation actually keeps more detail than summarization in every case
Because summarization eliminates the need for any token budget at all
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts summarization's compression-while-preserving-gist approach against truncation's outright discarding of old information, at a similar token cost.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against reaching for truncation as the default for every long-running agent?
options: Because it risks losing genuinely important early context purely because of age, not relevance
Because truncation is technically incapable of ever being implemented correctly
Because truncation always costs more than summarization or retrieval-based retention
Because truncation is only usable for tasks with no history at all
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is defaulting to truncation universally, when its indiscriminate dropping of old context can lose things that still matter, especially on longer tasks.

questions.question: Why does this lesson caution against picking retrieval-based retention for every task 'to be safe'?
options: Because its extra complexity is worth paying specifically for long, complex tasks — for shorter tasks, summarization or truncation is simpler and sufficient
Because retrieval-based retention is always strictly worse than truncation regardless of task length
Because retrieval-based retention cannot actually be implemented for any real agent
Because summarization and truncation are never adequate for any task, regardless of length
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is over-engineering with retrieval-based retention by default, when its added complexity is meant to be justified by genuinely long, complex tasks, not applied universally.

lessons.title: Scratchpads and Working Memory
lessons.description: Sometimes an agent needs a place to think and jot things down that isn't the same as its final answer.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what a scratchpad is for and how it differs from both the conversation history and the agent's final output.

sections.title: 📝 What a scratchpad is
sections.content: A dedicated space within the agent's state where it can write down intermediate calculations, partial results, hypotheses, or notes to itself — content that's useful for the agent's own ongoing reasoning but isn't meant to be shown to the end user or treated as a final answer. It's conceptually similar to a person's rough notes while working through a problem, as distinct from the polished final write-up.

sections.title: 🎯 Why separate this from the conversation itself
sections.content:
Mixing scratch reasoning directly into what gets shown to a user creates a messy, confusing experience — half-formed thoughts and abandoned approaches presented as if they were the final answer. Keeping a separate scratchpad lets the agent reason as messily and iteratively as it needs to internally, while still producing a clean, considered final output for the user, similar to the reasoning-versus-final-answer separation used in the reflection lesson.

```python
state = {
    "goal": goal,
    "history": [],       # thoughts / actions / observations
    "scratchpad": [],    # internal notes, never shown to the user
}
state["scratchpad"].append("running_total = 142; still need tax and shipping")
```

sections.title: 🧮 Common uses
sections.content:
- Tracking intermediate calculations in a multi-step numeric task, so later steps can reference exact prior values rather than the model trying to recall an approximate number from earlier in a long context.
- Keeping a running list of sub-tasks completed versus remaining, functioning as an explicit checklist rather than something the model has to infer from scattered context each time.
- Recording hypotheses that were tried and rejected, so the agent doesn't waste steps re-trying an approach it already ruled out earlier in the same run.

sections.title: ⚖️ Scratchpad content is still part of the token budget
sections.content: Even though scratchpad content isn't shown to the end user, it's still part of what gets fed into subsequent LLM calls and therefore counts against context length and cost — the context-management strategies from the previous lesson (truncation, summarization, selective retention) apply to scratchpad content just as much as to the visible action/observation history.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Letting scratchpad content leak into the user-facing output.** The whole point of a separate scratchpad is to keep messy internal reasoning out of what the user sees — forgetting to filter it before presenting a final answer defeats that purpose.

**Treating scratchpad content as exempt from context management.** It still counts against the token budget like anything else in state, so a scratchpad left unmanaged on a long task grows into the same context-overflow problem the previous lesson addresses.

**Using the scratchpad as a substitute for structured state instead of a genuine working-notes space.** A running checklist of sub-tasks or a tracked running total belongs in the scratchpad as intended; treating it as a dumping ground for anything the model wants to write loses the clarity that made it useful in the first place.

questions.question: What is a scratchpad in the context of an agent's working memory?
options: The agent's final answer shown to the user
A dedicated space for intermediate calculations, hypotheses, and notes not meant to be shown to the end user
A record of every tool ever available to the agent
A separate model used only for reasoning
questions.explanation: A scratchpad holds the agent's internal working notes — useful for its own ongoing reasoning but not part of the polished final output presented to the user.

questions.question: Why is it useful to keep scratchpad reasoning separate from what's shown to the end user?
options: It makes the agent run without a stopping condition
It lets the agent reason messily and iteratively internally while still producing a clean final output
Users always want to see every intermediate step
It eliminates the need for a context window
questions.explanation: Separating internal, possibly messy reasoning from the final answer keeps the user-facing output clean and considered, similar to the reasoning-versus-answer split used in reflection.

questions.question: Why does scratchpad content still matter for cost and context length, even though it's not user-facing?
options: It doesn't matter at all — scratchpad content is free
It's still fed into subsequent LLM calls, so it counts against context length and cost just like visible history
Scratchpad content is automatically deleted after each step
Only user-facing content counts toward the context window
questions.explanation: Scratchpad notes are part of the state passed into future LLM calls, so the same context-management strategies (truncation, summarization, retrieval) apply to them too.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what field holds the agent's internal notes, separate from the visible history?
options: state['scratchpad']
state['history']
state['goal']
There is no separate field — everything is stored in one list
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example defines state with a separate 'scratchpad' key, distinct from 'history' and 'goal', specifically for internal notes never shown to the user.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what kind of content is appended to the scratchpad?
options: A running total and a note about what still needs to be calculated
The complete final answer intended for the user
A list of every available tool in the system
The original user-facing conversation transcript
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example appends 'running_total = 142; still need tax and shipping' to the scratchpad, illustrating a tracked intermediate calculation.

questions.question: Why does this lesson list 'recording hypotheses that were tried and rejected' as a common scratchpad use?
options: Because it prevents the agent from wasting steps re-trying an approach it already ruled out earlier in the same run
Because rejected hypotheses must always be shown to the end user for transparency
Because hypotheses are never actually useful to track during a task
Because this use case has no relationship to avoiding wasted effort
questions.explanation: The lesson explains this use case specifically in terms of avoiding wasted effort — tracking what's already been ruled out prevents redundant re-exploration.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against letting scratchpad content leak into the user-facing output?
options: Because the whole point of a separate scratchpad is to keep messy internal reasoning out of what the user sees
Because scratchpad content is always identical to the final answer anyway
Because leaking scratchpad content always improves the user's experience
Because scratchpads are incapable of containing any content relevant to the final answer
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is failing to filter scratchpad content before presenting the final output, undermining the clean separation the scratchpad is meant to provide.

questions.question: Why does this lesson caution against treating scratchpad content as exempt from context management?
options: Because it still counts against the token budget like anything else in state, and left unmanaged it grows into the same context-overflow problem as visible history
Because scratchpad content is stored completely outside of the model's context window
Because context-management strategies only ever apply to the visible action/observation history, never to internal notes
Because scratchpads are automatically capped in size with no additional management needed
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is assuming scratchpad content escapes the token-budget concerns of the previous lesson, when it's just as much a part of state as anything else fed to the model.

lessons.title: Persisting Agent State Across Sessions
lessons.description: When a task spans more time than a single continuous run, the agent needs to pick up exactly where it left off.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Describe what's needed to let an agent pause and later resume a task from where it stopped, across separate sessions.

sections.title: 🔌 Why this comes up
sections.content: Not every agent task finishes in one continuous run — a task might wait on a slow external process, need human approval before continuing, or simply span a longer real-world timeline than makes sense to hold open as a single live process. In all of these cases, the agent's state needs to survive being paused and later resumed, potentially much later and potentially by a different process entirely.

sections.title: 💾 What needs to be saved
sections.content:
The full working state at the point of pausing: the task's original goal, the history of thoughts/actions/observations so far (or its summarized/retained form, per the context-management lesson), and any scratchpad content — essentially a serialized snapshot of everything that was being fed into the LLM at each loop iteration, saved somewhere durable (a database, not just in-memory).

```python
def pause(state):
    db.save_checkpoint(task_id=state["task_id"], snapshot=serialize(state))

def resume(task_id):
    snapshot = db.load_checkpoint(task_id)
    return deserialize(snapshot)  # loop continues exactly where it left off
```

sections.title: ▶️ Resuming correctly
sections.content: On resume, that saved state is loaded back and fed into the loop exactly as if the run had never paused — the agent shouldn't be able to tell the difference between a loop that ran continuously and one that was paused and resumed, other than possibly needing to re-verify that any facts it retrieved before pausing are still current if a lot of time has passed.

sections.title: 🧯 A related but distinct need: human-in-the-loop pauses
sections.content: A common reason to pause deliberately (not just as a recovery from a crash) is to require human approval before a high-stakes action proceeds — the agent reaches a point where it wants to take an irreversible or sensitive action, persists its state, and waits for an explicit approval signal before resuming and actually executing that action. This pattern connects directly to the guardrails lesson later in this course, where approval gates are one of the key safety mechanisms for agents taking real-world actions.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Keeping paused state only in memory rather than durable storage.** A pause that only survives as long as the current process does isn't really a pause — it's a crash waiting to lose the task entirely.

**Resuming a long-paused task without re-verifying time-sensitive facts.** State that was accurate when the agent paused can go stale if enough real-world time passes before it resumes — treating a snapshot as permanently current risks acting on outdated information.

**Building crash recovery and human-approval pausing as two separate, incompatible mechanisms.** Both need the exact same underlying capability — serializing and restoring full working state — so building them as one general pause/resume mechanism avoids duplicating the same logic twice.

questions.question: Why might an agent's task need to be paused and resumed across separate sessions rather than completing in one continuous run?
options: Agents can never take more than one step
The task might wait on a slow external process or require human approval before continuing
Pausing is never actually needed for real agent tasks
Context windows make pausing unnecessary
questions.explanation: Real tasks sometimes need to wait on external events or explicit approval, which means the run can't simply continue uninterrupted and must be able to persist and resume.

questions.question: What needs to be saved for an agent to resume correctly after a pause?
options: Nothing — the agent starts over from scratch every time
A durable snapshot of the working state: the original goal, the history (or its retained form), and any scratchpad content
Only the final answer produced so far
The agent's underlying model weights
questions.explanation: A full serialized snapshot of what was being fed into the loop needs to be saved durably so the agent can resume as if it had never paused.

questions.question: What is a common deliberate reason to pause an agent, beyond crash recovery?
options: To reduce the number of available tools
To require human approval before a high-stakes or irreversible action proceeds
To permanently end the task with no further action possible
To reset the agent's long-term memory
questions.explanation: Pausing for explicit human approval before risky actions is a key safety pattern, connecting directly to the guardrails and approval-gate mechanisms covered later in this course.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what does the pause function do with the current state?
options: Serializes it and saves it as a checkpoint keyed by task_id in a database
Deletes it permanently with no way to recover it
Sends it directly to the end user as the final answer
Converts it into a brand new tool definition
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example shows pause calling db.save_checkpoint(task_id=..., snapshot=serialize(state)), durably storing the state rather than keeping it only in memory.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what does resume do with the loaded checkpoint?
options: Deserializes it so the loop can continue exactly where it left off
Discards it and starts a completely new task from scratch
Uses it only to log an error message
Passes it unchanged directly to the end user
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example shows resume calling deserialize(snapshot) and returning the result, restoring the exact state the loop needs to continue seamlessly.

questions.question: Why does this lesson say the agent might need to 're-verify that any facts it retrieved before pausing are still current' on resume?
options: Because if a lot of real-world time has passed since pausing, previously retrieved facts could have gone stale
Because retrieved facts are always permanently valid regardless of how much time has passed
Because re-verification is required only for tasks that never use any tools
Because resuming a task always automatically refreshes every fact without any extra step
questions.explanation: The lesson notes this as a possible extra step on resume specifically because time passing during a pause can make previously-retrieved information outdated.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against keeping paused state only in memory rather than durable storage?
options: Because a pause that only survives as long as the current process does isn't really a pause — it's a crash waiting to lose the task entirely
Because in-memory storage is always faster and therefore always preferable to a database
Because durable storage is never actually necessary for any agent task
Because in-memory state persists correctly even if the process itself restarts
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is treating in-memory state as sufficient for pausing, when only durable storage actually protects the paused task against a process restart or crash.

questions.question: Why does this lesson recommend building crash recovery and human-approval pausing as one general mechanism rather than two separate ones?
options: Because both need the exact same underlying capability — serializing and restoring full working state — so building one mechanism avoids duplicating the same logic twice
Because crash recovery and human-approval pausing are completely unrelated problems with no shared requirements
Because human-approval pausing never actually requires saving any state at all
Because building them separately is always simpler than building one shared mechanism
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is treating these as separate problems, when both are really the same pause/resume capability applied to different triggers, so one well-built mechanism serves both.
